why: Alertness and reaction-time gains from caffeine grow with dose across the 50-200 mg range.
source: Smith 2002 Food Chem Toxicol 40:1243; Lieberman et al. 1987 Psychopharmacology 92:308

why: Even 32-64 mg caffeine raises alertness, but 100 mg does so more.
source: Lieberman et al. 1987 Psychopharmacology 92:308; Smit & Rogers 2000 Psychopharmacology 152:167

why: Caffeine is anxiogenic mainly at high doses (~300-500 mg); a single coffee barely changes anxiety in healthy people.
source: Childs & de Wit 2006 Psychopharmacology 185:514; Smith 2002 Food Chem Toxicol 40:1243

why: Sedation from alcohol rises steeply with blood alcohol; four drinks make people much sleepier than two.
source: Holdstock & de Wit 1998 Alcohol Clin Exp Res 22:1903; Roehrs & Roth 2001 Sleep Med Rev 5:287

why: Attention and psychomotor impairment by alcohol is dose-dependent with blood alcohol concentration.
source: Holloway 1995 (NHTSA DOT HS 808 238) review of BAC and performance; Dry et al. 2012 Psychopharmacology 222:393

why: Feeling drunk/intoxicated (subjective 'high') scales with blood alcohol concentration.
source: Holdstock & de Wit 1998 Alcohol Clin Exp Res 22:1903; King et al. 2011 Arch Gen Psychiatry 68:389

why: Alcohol is biphasic: stimulating on the rising limb but sedating on the falling limb; at 3 h the drop in alertness is larger after the higher dose.
source: Martin et al. 1993 Alcohol Clin Exp Res 17:140 (Biphasic Alcohol Effects Scale); Holdstock & de Wit 1998

why: Subjective high and perceptual change from smoked THC increase with dose.
source: Hart et al. 2001 Neuropsychopharmacology 25:757; Chait & Zacny 1992 Psychopharmacology 107:255

why: Cannabinoids are biphasic for anxiety: low THC doses can be calming or neutral, high doses reliably cause anxiety and paranoia.
source: Childs, Lutz & de Wit 2017 Drug Alcohol Depend 177:136 (7.5 mg vs 12.5 mg THC); D'Souza et al. 2004 Neuropsychopharmacology 29:1558

why: Opioid pain relief follows a graded dose-response in the clinical range.
source: Goodman & Gilman's Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, opioid chapter; Walsh et al. 2008 Clin Pharmacol Ther

why: Respiratory depression by mu-opioids increases with dose without a ceiling.
source: Dahan et al. 2010 Anesthesiology 112:226; Pattinson 2008 Br J Anaesth 100:747

why: A double heroin dose produces much deeper respiratory depression; this is the mechanism of overdose.
source: Dahan et al. 2010 Anesthesiology 112:226; White & Irvine 1999 Addiction 94:961

why: Rated euphoria/drug liking from heroin increases with dose.
source: Comer et al. 1999 Psychopharmacology 143:327; Jones et al. 2011 Drug Alcohol Depend

why: Sedation from diazepam is clearly greater at 10 mg than 5 mg.
source: de Visser et al. 2003 Br J Clin Pharmacol 55:39 (benzodiazepine dose-effect review); Mattila et al. 1988

why: Anxiolysis from diazepam is dose-related, though 2.5 mg has small effects in non-anxious people.
source: Goodman & Gilman's, benzodiazepine chapter; de Visser et al. 2003 Br J Clin Pharmacol 55:39

why: Stimulant-like subjective effects and alertness rise with methylphenidate dose.
source: Kollins et al. 1998 Exp Clin Psychopharmacol 6:367; Volkow et al. 1999 Am J Psychiatry 156:1440

why: Euphoria/'good drug effect' from MDMA is dose-dependent between 50 and 125 mg.
source: Harris et al. 2002 Psychopharmacology 162:396; Kirkpatrick et al. 2014 Psychopharmacology

why: Feelings of closeness and sociability grow with MDMA dose.
source: Kirkpatrick et al. 2014 Psychopharmacology 231:2161; Bershad et al. 2016

why: Altered-state ratings (5D-ASC) from psilocybin are strongly dose-dependent.
source: Hasler et al. 2004 Psychopharmacology 172:145; Griffiths et al. 2011 Psychopharmacology 218:649

why: Subjective stimulation from nicotine rises with dose, though nausea limits higher doses in non-users.
source: Perkins et al. 1994 Psychopharmacology 115:185; Heishman et al. 2010 Psychopharmacology 210:453

why: A recreational methamphetamine dose (often 25-100 mg, partly smoked/injected) stimulates far more than 10 mg oral dexamphetamine.
source: Mendelson et al. 2006 Clin Pharmacol Ther 80:403; Kirkpatrick et al. 2012 Psychopharmacology

why: Methamphetamine is a far stronger wakefulness promoter than a coffee.
source: Hart et al. 2008 Psychopharmacology 196:571; Smith 2002 Food Chem Toxicol

why: A street dose of injected/smoked heroin hits the brain fast and hard; 10 mg oral morphine causes only mild respiratory slowing.
source: Dahan et al. 2010 Anesthesiology 112:226; Darke & Hall 2003 J Urban Health 80:189

why: Rapid-onset injected heroin gives an intense rush; oral morphine gives mild, slow euphoria.
source: Comer et al. 1999 Psychopharmacology 143:327; de Wit et al. 1992 on rate of delivery and euphoria

why: Intranasal cocaine produces marked euphoria; caffeine only slight mood lift.
source: Fischman et al. 1976 Arch Gen Psychiatry; Smit & Rogers 2000 Psychopharmacology 152:167

why: Cocaine strongly raises drive and 'wanting' through large striatal dopamine release; caffeine's effect is modest.
source: Volkow et al. 1997 Nature 386:827; Volkow et al. 2015 Transl Psychiatry (caffeine)

why: Psilocybin produces full psychedelic perceptual changes; a moderate joint gives mild perceptual alteration.
source: Hasler et al. 2004 Psychopharmacology 172:145; D'Souza et al. 2004 Neuropsychopharmacology 29:1558

why: 100 µg LSD causes strong visual and perceptual alterations, well beyond a moderate joint.
source: Schmid et al. 2015 Biol Psychiatry 78:544; Holze et al. 2021 Neuropsychopharmacology

why: Sub-anaesthetic ketamine produces clear dissociative and perceptual changes (CADSS); two drinks do not.
source: Krystal et al. 1994 Arch Gen Psychiatry 51:199; Krystal et al. 1998 (ketamine vs ethanol)

why: MDMA's perceptual changes are mild compared with psilocybin's.
source: Liechti et al. 2001 Neuropsychopharmacology; Holze et al. 2020 Neuropsychopharmacology 45:462 (MDMA vs LSD)

why: MDMA strongly increases feelings of closeness and trust; alcohol mainly increases talkativeness.
source: Kirkpatrick & de Wit 2015 Psychopharmacology 232:1155; Dolder et al. 2018 Front Pharmacol 9:1258

why: In head-to-head studies MDMA raised closeness and empathy, methylphenidate did not.
source: Hysek et al. 2014 Soc Cogn Affect Neurosci 9:1645; Schmid et al. 2014 Psychopharmacology

why: Diazepam reliably dampens stress-induced anxiety; theanine's effect is small and inconsistent.
source: Hoffman et al. 2005 benzodiazepine stress studies; Williams et al. 2020 Plant Foods Hum Nutr 75:12 (theanine review)

why: Opioids give robust analgesia; THC's effect on acute pain is weak and inconsistent.
source: Kraft et al. 2008 Anesthesiology 109:101; Whiting et al. 2015 JAMA 313:2456

why: Benzodiazepines alone barely depress breathing in healthy people; heroin strongly does.
source: White & Irvine 1999 Addiction 94:961; Gueye et al. 2002 Toxicol Sci

why: Cocaine euphoria is much stronger than the mild pleasure of one cigarette in a non-smoker.
source: Volkow et al. 1997 Nature 386:827; Perkins et al. 1994 Psychopharmacology 115:185

why: Caffeine raises alertness; theanine alone does not and may even relax.
source: Haskell et al. 2008 Biol Psychol 77:113; Owen et al. 2008 Nutr Neurosci 11:193

why: Naloxone blocks mu-opioid receptors and reverses opioid respiratory depression.
source: Dahan et al. 2010 Anesthesiology 112:226; Goodman & Gilman's

why: Methylphenidate improves attention in both groups, but gains are larger in ADHD where baseline attention is lower.
source: Faraone 2009 P&T 34:678; Ilieva et al. 2015 J Cogn Neurosci 27:1069 (small effects in healthy)

why: Caffeine's alerting effect is larger when there is sleep debt to counteract.
source: Smith 2002 Food Chem Toxicol; McLellan, Caldwell & Lieberman 2016 Neurosci Biobehav Rev 71:294

why: People with anxiety disorders are more sensitive to caffeine's anxiogenic effect.
source: Boulenger et al. 1984 Arch Gen Psychiatry 41:1067; Charney et al. 1985 Arch Gen Psychiatry 42:233

why: Anxious individuals appear more prone to THC-induced anxiety and panic.
source: Crippa et al. 2009 Hum Psychopharmacol 24:515; Sharpe et al. 2020 Neurosci Biobehav Rev

why: Ketamine's next-day mood lift is a robust antidepressant effect in depression but absent in healthy people.
source: Zarate et al. 2006 Arch Gen Psychiatry 63:856; Krystal et al. 2019 Neuron

why: Propranolol blocks the bodily fear response, so it lowers anxiety mainly during stress; at rest it does little.
source: Steenen et al. 2016 J Psychopharmacol 30:128; Brantigan et al. 1982 Am J Med 72:88

why: At 22:00 sleep pressure is high, so caffeine has more sleepiness to remove than mid-morning.
source: Landolt et al. 1995 Brain Res; Drake et al. 2013 J Clin Sleep Med 9:1195

why: Habitual users largely just reverse withdrawal; their state is close to never-users, so the net gain is small.
source: James & Rogers 2005 Psychopharmacology 182:1; Rogers et al. 2013 Psychopharmacology 226:229

why: Regular smokers develop tolerance; smoking mainly relieves withdrawal rather than raising them above non-smokers.
source: Parrott 1999 Am Psychol 54:817; Perkins 1995 Psychopharmacology

why: Analgesic tolerance builds with weeks of daily opioid use, and hyperalgesia can appear.
source: Chu et al. 2006 J Pain 7:43; Morgan & Christie 2011 Br J Pharmacol 164:1322

why: Daily heroin users show large tolerance to euphoria and mostly dose to avoid withdrawal.
source: Koob & Le Moal 2005 Nat Neurosci 8:1442; Comer et al. 1999 Psychopharmacology 143:327

why: Tolerance to the sedative effect of benzodiazepines develops within days to weeks.
source: Ashton 1994 Drugs 48:25; Vinkers & Olivier 2012 Adv Pharmacol Sci

why: Some tolerance to anxiolysis develops with weeks of use, though slower than for sedation.
source: Ashton 1994 Drugs 48:25; Lader 2011 Addiction 106:2086

why: Regular drinkers show tolerance to alcohol's sedative effects.
source: King et al. 2011 Arch Gen Psychiatry 68:389 (heavy vs light drinkers); Kalant 1998 Alcohol Clin Exp Res

why: SSRIs lift mood in depression only after weeks; a first dose does not.
source: Cipriani et al. 2018 Lancet 391:1357; Taylor et al. 2006 Arch Gen Psychiatry 63:1217

why: Semaglutide reaches steady state over weeks of dose escalation; appetite suppression is large at maintenance but small hours after a first injection.
source: Blundell et al. 2017 Diabetes Obes Metab 19:1242; Friedrichsen et al. 2021 Diabetes Obes Metab 23:754

why: Alcohol adds to opioid respiratory depression and is present in a large share of heroin overdose deaths.
source: van der Schrier et al. 2017 Anesthesiology 126:534; Darke & Hall 2003 J Urban Health 80:189

why: Benzodiazepines potentiate opioid respiratory depression (FDA boxed warning).
source: FDA 2016 Drug Safety Communication; Hernandez et al. 2018 JAMA Netw Open

why: Alcohol and benzodiazepines are additive or supra-additive for sedation.
source: Linnoila et al. 1990 Alcohol Alcohol; Tanaka 2002 J Toxicol Clin Toxicol 40:69

why: Adding cocaine to alcohol increases euphoria (cocaethylene forms) beyond alcohol alone.
source: McCance-Katz et al. 1993 Biol Psychiatry 34:525; Farré et al. 1993 J Pharmacol Exp Ther 266:1364

why: Cocaine offsets alcohol's sedation, which is why the combination feels less drunk.
source: Farré et al. 1993 J Pharmacol Exp Ther 266:1364; Pennings et al. 2002 Addiction 97:773

why: Cannabis and alcohol impair attention and driving performance additively.
source: Hartman et al. 2015 Addiction 110:1604; Ramaekers et al. 2000 Drug Alcohol Depend 57:57
